titles.1: Basic Principles of Life and Health Insurance
titles.11: Florida Health Laws, Rules, and Regulations

questions.q: Which type of insurer is owned by its policyholders and typically issues participating policies?
questions.w: Mutuals are owned by policyholders and issue par policies that may pay dividends.

questions.q: A life insurance policy that pays a predetermined amount regardless of the actual loss is a:
questions.w: Life policies are valued contracts; most accident, health, property, and casualty contracts are indemnity contracts.

questions.q: Who represents the insured rather than the insurer and cannot bind coverage?
questions.w: Agents represent insurers; brokers represent insureds.

questions.q: An insurer incorporated in Georgia is licensed to do business in Florida. In Florida it is a:
questions.w: Foreign means incorporated in another U.S. state. Alien means incorporated outside the U.S.

questions.q: In a reinsurance agreement, the company that transfers its risk is called the:
questions.w: The ceding (primary) insurer transfers risk and stays responsible to the client.

questions.q: Reinsurance arranged case by case to cover one specific risk is:
questions.w: Treaty reinsurance is automatic and broad; facultative is for a specific risk.

questions.q: Which organization is made up of subscribers who insure each other through an attorney-in-fact?
questions.w: Reciprocals are unincorporated risk-sharing arrangements run by an attorney-in-fact.

questions.q: Which is NOT a required trait of a fraternal benefit society?
o: Exists for reasons other than insurance
questions.w: Fraternals must be non-profit, have a lodge system and representative government, and exist for more than insurance.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a risk retention group and a risk purchasing group?
o: RPGs buy insurance from an insurer; RRGs act as insurers
RPGs are licensed in every state
RRGs were created by the NAIC
questions.w: Both come from the LRRA of 1986, but an RPG is a master policyholder, not an insurer.

questions.q: Lloyd's of London is best described as:
o: A syndicate of individuals and companies that underwrite insurance
questions.w: Lloyd's is not an insurer; it is a marketplace compared to the New York Stock Exchange.

questions.q: Which Supreme Court decision held that insurance is interstate commerce subject to federal regulation?
questions.w: McCarran-Ferguson then returned primary regulation to the states in 1945.

questions.q: Under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, sharing protected health information requires:
o: Nothing, if the party is affiliated
questions.w: General sharing with non-affiliated third parties is opt-out; health information needs opt-in.

questions.q: Which statement about the NAIC is true?
o: It enforces compliance in each state
It writes model acts and regulations
questions.w: The NAIC is not a regulator. NCOIL, made up of state legislators, was formed in 1969.

questions.q: In which agency system do agents own their book of business and represent many insurers?
questions.w: The independent agency system came from the property and casualty industry.

questions.q: Under the CAN-SPAM Act, opt-out requests must be honored within:
questions.w: Email must also have accurate headers, be labeled as advertising, and include a physical address.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a rating service such as A.M. Best is to:
questions.w: Ratings look at reserves and liquidity. Rating services are not technically oversight.

questions.q: Who is NOT licensed to sell insurance but solicits applicants on behalf of a producer?
questions.w: A service representative also needs no license unless they take commissions, solicit, countersign, or collect premiums.

questions.q: Which type of risk is insurable?
questions.w: Only pure risks (loss only) are insurable

questions.q: An applicant who knows they have a serious health condition applies for coverage without disclosing it. This is an example of:
questions.w: Concealing material information is adverse selection

questions.q: A homeowner rarely changes smoke detector batteries because the house is insured. This is a:
questions.w: Careless because insured = morale

questions.q: Which principle prevents insurance from being a source of profit?
questions.w: Indemnity restores, never profits

questions.q: Which type of policy is NOT subject to the principle of indemnity?
questions.w: Life insurance is a valued contract

questions.q: A policy that covers all direct causes of loss except those it excludes is a:
questions.w: Open (special) peril covers everything not excluded

questions.q: Every accident is an occurrence, but:
o: Not every occurrence is an accident
questions.w: Occurrences can be gradual, accidents are sudden

questions.q: The law of large numbers requires all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.w: One location breaks independence (one flood hits all)

questions.q: A company decides not to build in a flood zone. Which method of handling risk is this?
questions.w: Eliminating the activity = avoidance

questions.q: A $1,000 deductible on an auto policy is an example of:
questions.w: Deductibles are retention

questions.q: An 80/20 coinsurance split in a major medical policy is an example of:
questions.w: Coinsurance spreads the cost between parties

questions.q: Faking medical symptoms to collect disability benefits is a:
questions.w: Intentional and dishonest = moral

questions.q: An applicant judged to have a higher-than-average potential for loss is classified as:
questions.w: Substandard = higher risk, higher premium or lower benefit

questions.q: Which is the most complete form of risk management?
questions.w: Avoidance eliminates the risk completely

questions.q: A loss that results from a direct loss, rather than straight from the peril, is called:
questions.w: Indirect loss is also called consequential loss

questions.q: Insurers use reinsurance mainly to:
questions.w: Reinsurance transfers risk to other insurers to prevent catastrophic loss

questions.q: High blood pressure noted on a medical exam is a:
questions.w: Can be measured or documented = physical

questions.q: Who are the parties to an insurance contract?
questions.w: Only the policy owner (applicant) and insurer; the insured and beneficiary aren't parties.

questions.q: An applicant completes an online application but does not submit a premium. What has happened?
questions.w: An application without premium is only an invitation.

questions.q: A 16-year-old buys a life policy without parental consent. The contract is:
questions.w: A minor lacks competence, so the contract is void from the beginning.

questions.q: Which feature means only the insurer makes an enforceable promise?
questions.w: Unilateral: the applicant doesn't even promise to pay premiums.

questions.q: A policy term is ambiguous. A court will typically:
questions.w: Contract of adhesion: the insurer wrote it, so ambiguities favor the insured.

questions.q: Which contract is NOT a personal contract because ownership can be assigned?
questions.w: Life insurance is the exception; it can be assigned by notifying the insurer in writing.

questions.q: A $500,000 life policy pays $500,000 at death regardless of actual loss. This is a:
questions.w: Valued contract; life insurance is always valued.

questions.q: For life insurance, insurable interest must exist:
questions.w: Life and health: only at application. Property and casualty: application and loss.

questions.q: A statement on a life application that is substantially true when made is a:
questions.w: Representations are substantially true when made; warranties are exactly true throughout.

questions.q: An applicant knowingly leaves out a recent heart attack when asked about medical history. This is:
questions.w: Concealment is failing to disclose a known, material fact.

questions.q: An agent prints business cards with the company name, though the contract doesn't mention it. This is:
questions.w: Implied authority is unwritten but necessary to do the job.

questions.q: Most agent mistakes that create insurer liability fall under:
questions.w: Apparent authority.

questions.q: Before a policy is issued, an agent says it covers all water damage; the policy excludes flood. Which rule says the written policy wins?
questions.w: Parole evidence rule: only written terms bind; it covers statements made before the policy.

questions.q: Which can bind coverage?
questions.w: Only the agent; brokers and solicitors cannot bind.

questions.q: Your insurer pays $5,000 for damage caused by another driver, then collects from that driver's insurer. This is:
questions.w: Subrogation: the insurer steps into your shoes.

questions.q: Which type of negligence is NOT covered by E&O?
questions.w: Willful and wanton is not covered; gross is sometimes covered; simple is usually covered.

questions.q: The two perils covered by health and accident insurance are:
questions.w: Accidents and sickness are the two perils

questions.q: The risk of becoming ill or disabled is called:
questions.w: Morbidity = illness or disability risk; mortality = death

questions.q: Robert voluntarily jumps from a height and is injured. Which definition would pay his claim?
questions.w: The jump was voluntary, so accidental means pays nothing

questions.q: Under an AD&D policy, the death benefit is the:
questions.w: Principal sum = death benefit = face amount

questions.q: On the exam, the standard percentage of the principal sum paid as a capital sum is:
questions.w: Exam Tip: assume 50%

questions.q: If an exam question asks the time frame within which an accidental death must occur, assume:
questions.w: Exam Tip: assume 90 days

questions.q: An AD&D policy pays $50,000 for loss of life. What does it typically pay for loss of one leg?
questions.w: One arm or leg = two-thirds of the principal sum

questions.q: Which pays a lump sum on diagnosis and survival of a heart attack, usable for any expense?
questions.w: Critical illness pays a lump sum on diagnosis and survival

questions.q: Hospital indemnity benefits are based on:
questions.w: Paid on days confined, not on expenses

questions.q: In credit disability insurance, the policy owner and beneficiary is the:
questions.w: Creditor is owner and beneficiary; debtor is the insured

questions.q: A school covering its sports teams, whose players change each season, would buy:
questions.w: Same risk, changing members = blanket

questions.q: Short-term medical policies:
o: Last up to 12 months and renew automatically
Last up to 90 days and cannot be renewed
questions.w: Up to 90 days, not renewable

questions.q: Under a non-scheduled dental plan, basic services such as fillings are typically paid at:
Which dental specialty treats gum disease?
questions.w: Periodontics = gums

questions.q: Long-term care insurance would NOT cover care needed because of:
questions.w: Psychological conditions are excluded; LTC requires an organic cause

questions.q: What must a limited benefit policy give the policyholder?
questions.w: States require a Notice to Insured on limited policies

questions.q: A health plan that pays a fixed amount per member to providers, regardless of how much care the member uses, is paying by:
questions.w: Capitation = per patient, not per service.

questions.q: Which HMO model has physicians working in their own offices on a part-time basis and offers members the broadest choice of providers?
questions.w: IPA = open panel, own offices, part-time, broadest choice.

questions.q: Under which HMO model are physicians salaried employees of the HMO?
questions.w: Staff model physicians are employed and salaried by the HMO.

questions.q: Blue Shield primarily covers:
questions.w: Blue Cross = hospital; Blue Shield = surgical and medical.

questions.q: A nurse monitors a patient's hospital stay to decide when the patient can be released or moved to an extended care facility. This is:
questions.w: Concurrent review happens while care is provided.

questions.q: Which plan allows members to see in-network specialists without a referral, but provides no out-of-network coverage except in an actual emergency?
questions.w: EPO: no referrals, no out-of-network except emergencies.

questions.q: A noncontributory group health plan typically requires what level of participation by eligible employees?
questions.w: Noncontributory = 100%.

questions.q: An employer has 400 eligible employees and offers a contributory plan. Under general guidelines, how many must enroll?
Large groups (51 or more members) are generally underwritten using:
questions.w: Large = experience; small (2–50) = community.

questions.q: Which arrangement issues individual policies to members of an association, with the association acting only as the sponsor?
questions.w: Franchise (wholesale) plans issue individual policies.

questions.q: Under a Multiple Employer Trust (MET), who holds the master contract?
questions.w: The MET holds the master contract, not the employers.

questions.q: COBRA applies to employers with at least how many employees?
questions.w: COBRA groups = 20 or more employees.

questions.q: An employee voluntarily resigns. How long can COBRA continuation last?
questions.w: Loss of employment = 18 months.

questions.q: A former employee's share of the group premium was $200 and the total monthly group premium is $500. What is the maximum COBRA premium?
Under HIPAA, prior coverage counts as creditable coverage only if there was no gap of:
questions.w: A gap of 63 days or more breaks creditable coverage.

questions.q: An employee's spouse is covered under the group plan and the couple divorces. How long can the spouse keep COBRA coverage?
questions.w: Divorce is a dependent event = 36 months.

questions.q: How soon after a qualifying event must an employer notify the employee of COBRA rights?
questions.w: Notice within 14 days; then 60 days to elect.

questions.q: The Pregnancy Discrimination Act applies to employers with at least:
questions.w: PDA covers employers with 15 or more employees.

questions.q: A covered employee is hospitalized when their group membership ends. The plan keeps paying for that hospital stay but not for any new illness. This is:
questions.w: Extension of benefits covers existing claims only.

questions.q: An employee who misses the 31-day enrollment period and applies later must generally:
questions.w: Late enrollees must show evidence of insurability.

questions.q: Alfred has a minor surgery during a hospital stay. Which cost would his basic hospital policy cover?
questions.w: Basic hospital covers things billed by the hospital, including nursing staff. The anesthesiologist and attending physician bill on their own (surgical / physician policies)

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of basic medical expense insurance?
o: A significant annual deductible with coinsurance
questions.w: Deductibles and coinsurance belong to major medical. Basic is first-dollar

questions.q: A basic surgical policy uses a relative value scale of $100 per unit. A knee arthroscopy is worth 26 units. What does the policy pay the surgeon?
The UCR charge for a procedure is $2,000 and the policy pays 80% of UCR. The surgeon bills $2,400. How much does the insured pay?
questions.w: Insurer pays 80% × $2,000 UCR = $1,600. Insured pays $2,400 − $1,600 = $800

questions.q: Covered expenses are $7,000. A basic policy pays the first $4,000. The major medical deductible is $5,000 and is integrated. How much does the insured pay?
questions.w: Basic's $4,000 counts toward the $5,000 integrated deductible; insured pays the last $1,000; major medical pays $2,000

questions.q: Same facts as question 5, but the $5,000 deductible is a corridor deductible. How much does the insured pay?
questions.w: Basic pays $4,000, leaving $3,000; the insured owes up to $5,000 in the corridor, so pays all $3,000

questions.q: A policy has a $500 deductible and 80/20 coinsurance. The insured has a $3,000 covered claim. How much does the insurer pay?
A policy has a $1,000 deductible, 80/20 coinsurance and a $3,000 stop-loss. The insured has a $25,000 covered claim. How much does the insurer pay?
A family of four has a $500 individual and $1,000 family deductible. Each member has $250 of covered claims. What happens next?
o: Nothing is paid until one member reaches $500
The family deductible is met, so the insurer pays the next covered claim
Each member must still pay $250 more
questions.w: $250 × 4 = $1,000 meets the family deductible even though no one met the individual one

questions.q: Which provision lets claims from the last three months of the year count toward next year's deductible?
questions.w: The carryover provision covers the final three months of the policy year

questions.q: A buyer wants a Marketplace plan where they expect to pay about 20% of covered costs. Which tier fits?
questions.w: Gold = 80% actuarial value, so the insured pays about 20%

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the ACA's 10 essential health benefits?
o: Mental health and substance use disorder services
questions.w: Pediatric dental and vision are mandatory; adult dental and vision are optional

questions.q: Under HIPAA, an employee with 8 months of creditable coverage (no gap) joins a group plan with a 12-month pre-existing condition exclusion. How long is the remaining exclusion?
questions.w: Each month of creditable coverage cancels a month: 12 − 8 = 4 months

questions.q: Which expense is NOT a qualified HSA expense?
questions.w: Medicare expenses qualify, but Medigap does not

questions.q: Which account does NOT require a high-deductible health plan?
questions.w: Unlike the other accounts, an FSA does not require an HDHP

questions.q: Maria itemizes, has an AGI of $60,000 and $6,000 of medical expenses. How much can she deduct?
A policy considers an insured disabled if they can't perform the material and substantial duties of their regular job, even if they could work elsewhere. This is:
questions.w: Own occupation = can't do your own job, even if you could do another.

questions.q: Which definition of disability is used by Social Security?
questions.w: SGA is the Social Security definition.

questions.q: Under the Social Security definition, the disability must be expected to result in death or last at least:
questions.w: Death, or lasted / expected to last 12 continuous months.

questions.q: Bob's policy pays $1,000/month with a 30-day waiting period. He's out 5 months, returns to work for 3 months, then relapses with the same condition for 4 months. How many months of benefits are paid?
questions.w: 4 months (after the 1-month wait) + 4 months (relapse within 6 months, no new wait) = 8.

questions.q: An insured earns $4,000/month and has a total disability benefit of 60% of income. Using the course's standard partial benefit, what is the monthly partial disability benefit?
Frank earns $5,000/month and has a total disability benefit of $3,500. A disability reduces his income by 40%. What is his residual benefit?
Which of the following automatically qualifies as a presumptive disability?
o: A broken leg expected to heal in 4 months
Total and permanent loss of hearing
A back injury preventing full-time work
questions.w: Presumptive: double dismemberment or permanent loss of sight, hearing, or speech.

questions.q: What is the SSDI waiting period?
questions.w: 5 months; benefits accrue in month 6.

questions.q: Which statement about the probationary period is correct?
o: It applies to each disability claim
It occurs once, at policy inception, and excludes illness
It is common in group plans
questions.w: One time at the start; accidents are covered, illness isn't. Group plans usually don't have one.

questions.q: An insured changes to a less hazardous occupation without telling the insurer. Under the change of occupation provision, the insurer will:
questions.w: Less hazardous = premium reduced (not the benefit).

questions.q: Which renewal provision allows the insurer to raise premiums, but only for an entire class of policyholders?
questions.w: Guaranteed renewable: premiums can rise by class only.

questions.q: Which rider lets the insured buy more disability coverage at future dates without proof of good health?
questions.w: Guaranteed insurability (FIO / APO / GPO).

questions.q: On a life insurance policy, the disability income rider typically pays:
o: 1% of the face amount per month
2% of the face amount per month
questions.w: 1% of face amount, up to $1,000.

questions.q: A business owner wants coverage for rent, utilities, and employee salaries if the owner becomes disabled. The best product is:
questions.w: BOE covers operating expenses, not the owner's income.

questions.q: A partnership has 4 partners and uses a cross-purchase disability buy-out plan. How many policies are needed?
An employer pays the full premium for group disability insurance. How are the employee's benefits taxed?
questions.w: Employer-paid premium is deductible, so benefits are taxable.

questions.q: Group STD plans typically have a maximum benefit period of:
questions.w: Group STD: no more than 26 weeks (13 where allowed by law).

questions.q: For an exam question asking whether group disability insurance is occupational or non-occupational, the course suggests choosing:
questions.w: Exam tip: choose non-occupational.

questions.note:
#### Notes on conflicting course numbers
The course gives two different figures in a few places. Both are listed above so you recognize either on the exam:
- **Probationary period:** keyword page says 7 to 30 days; section 5.1.1 says 15, 30, or 60 days.
- **Return of premium rider:** keyword page says a dollar-for-dollar refund without interest if no claim is filed; section 5.5.8 says a percentage of premiums with favorable claims, at 65 or every 5 or 10 years.
- **Cash surrender value rider:** section says all premiums at 65 less benefits received; review keywords say all premiums at 65 if no claims have been made.

---

questions.q: An employee turns 65 and is still working for a company with 50 employees, covered by its group health plan. Which is true?
o: The group plan is primary and Part B can be delayed without penalty
The employee must enroll in Part B within 7 months or pay a penalty
The employer can pay the employee to drop group coverage
questions.w: 20+ employees = COBRA group. Group is primary; Part B can wait until the SEP. Employers can't pay workers to drop coverage.

questions.q: A person under 65 diagnosed with ALS becomes eligible for Medicare:
questions.w: ALS has no waiting period.

questions.q: A person with ESRD who also has group health coverage through a spouse's employer. For how long is the group plan primary?
questions.w: Group plan primary for the first 30 months.

questions.q: A person's 65th birthday is in October. Their Initial Enrollment Period runs:
o: July 1 to the last day of January
questions.w: 3 months before, birth month, 3 months after.

questions.q: Someone delays Part B for 24 months with no group coverage. Their Part B premium penalty is:
questions.w: 10% for each full 12 months: 2 × 10% = 20%, for life.

questions.q: Jane was hospitalized for 92 days in one benefit period. How many lifetime reserve days remain?
questions.w: 90 basic days + 2 reserve days used. 60 − 2 = 58. Reserve days don't come back.

questions.q: A patient is discharged from the hospital and readmitted 45 days later for a related condition. Medicare treats this as:
questions.w: Readmission within 60 days of discharge continues the same benefit period.

questions.q: To qualify for Part A skilled nursing facility care, the patient must first have:
questions.w: At least 3 inpatient days, same condition.

questions.q: A patient receives 4 pints of blood as a hospital inpatient. No donations were made. The patient pays for:
questions.w: Exam tip: assume the insured pays the first 3 pints unless donations are mentioned.

questions.q: A nonparticipating provider may charge a Medicare patient up to how much above the Medicare-approved amount?
questions.w: Up to 15% more.

questions.q: A beneficiary wants to appeal a denied claim shown on their Medicare Summary Notice. They have:
questions.w: 120 days from receiving the MSN.

questions.q: Which of these is covered by Medicare Part B?
questions.w: DME is Part B. Dental, outpatient drugs, and custodial care are excluded.

questions.q: To join a Medicare Advantage plan, a person must:
o: Be enrolled in Part A only
Be enrolled in Parts A and B and live in the plan's service area
questions.w: Must have A and B, keep paying the Part B premium, and live in the service area.

questions.q: Which Medigap plan contains only the core benefits?
questions.w: Plan A = core benefits only.

questions.q: For someone first eligible for Medicare in 2024, which Medigap plan is closest to Plan F?
questions.w: G mirrors F minus the Part B deductible, for people new to Medicare after 2020.

questions.q: The Medigap open enrollment period lasts:
o: 6 months, starting when the person is 65 and enrolled in Part B
questions.w: 6 months, starting the month you're both 65 and in Part B.

questions.q: An agent earns $300 first-year commission on a Medigap sale. The minimum second-year commission is:
questions.w: First year can't exceed 200% of year two, so year two is at least $150.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the six ADLs?
questions.w: ADLs: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, eating.

questions.q: An LTC policy pays a fixed daily indemnity of $150. The insured's covered costs one day are $120. The policy pays:
questions.w: Indemnity pays the stated amount regardless of cost.

questions.q: An LTC policy has a $200 daily maximum and a 2-year benefit period. What is the pool of money?
Which feature is required for a tax-qualified (HIPAA) LTC policy?
questions.w: HIPAA requires a 30-day free look; no cash surrender value; no prior hospital stay.

questions.q: The LTC level of care that is intermittent and provided by skilled personnel on a doctor's orders is:
questions.w: Intermediate = intermittent, skilled personnel, doctor's orders.

questions.q: A Long-Term Care Partnership policy must be:
questions.w: Partnership policies must be tax-qualified and include inflation protection.

questions.note:
#### Notes on conflicting course content

The course says different things in a few places. Both versions are listed so you recognize either on the exam.

- **Part D and Medicare Advantage.** Section 3.4 says MA members are **ineligible** for Part D and that enrolling in Part D **ends** an MA plan. But the overview, section 2.4.4, and the review notes say Part D can be **included in** MA plans and MA members can choose a plan with Part D for extra premium. The way they fit together: drug coverage comes either as a stand-alone PDP (with Original Medicare) or built into an MA plan. You can't hold a stand-alone PDP and an MA plan at the same time.
- **ESRD and Medicare Advantage.** Section 3.3.1 says MA enrollees must **not** have ESRD, but section 3.3.2.4 says Special Needs Plans serve people with chronic conditions **such as ESRD**.
- **SNF deductible.** The text says the first 20 SNF days are fully covered with **no deductible**. The Part A summary table says "100% after the deductible / patient pays deductible."
- **Medigap Part A deductible and SNF coinsurance.** The text (and review notes) say every plan except A covers the Part A deductible and every plan except A and B covers SNF coinsurance. The chart shows **K (50%), L (75%), and M (50% for the Part A deductible)** cover only part.
- **Medigap look-back period.** Section 4.1 says the 6-month look-back "runs from the policy's effective date." Section 4.3 says it is the 6 months **immediately preceding** the effective date.
- **Pool of money math.** Section 5.6.2 says 365 × $100 = **$35,600**. The correct product is **$36,500**. The pool-of-money concept still holds.
- **Plan N.** The 2025 chart in the screenshot ends at Plan M, but the review notes list Plan N (foreign travel, Part B coinsurance with copays).
- **Automatic inflation rider.** The keyword page says it raises the **face amount** about 5% a year. The section says it raises the **stated daily benefit**, compounded annually.
- **PFFS and networks.** The review notes list PFFS among MA "provider networks," but section 3.3.2.3 says PFFS lets you see **any** Medicare-approved provider that accepts its payment.
- **Part A late penalty.** Section 2.4.1 says only that the penalty depends on the length of delay. The review notes give the rule: **10% for twice the number of years delayed**.

---

questions.q: Which provision is mandatory under the NAIC model law?
questions.w: Grace period is one of the 12 mandatory; the others are optional.

questions.q: A health policy with monthly premiums must have a grace period of at least:
questions.w: 7 weekly, **10 monthly**, 31 other.

questions.q: Under the NAIC Model Act, an insured must give notice of claim within:
questions.w: 20 days.

questions.q: The insurer fails to send claim forms within 15 days of notice. The insured may:
o: Submit proof of loss in any reasonable form, which the insurer must accept
Cancel the policy for a full refund
questions.w: Insured may submit proof any way; insurer must accept.

questions.q: An insured may not sue the insurer over a claim until how long after submitting proof of loss?
questions.w: 60 days after proof of loss (and within 3 years).

questions.q: A lapsed policy is reinstated. Which is covered first?
o: An illness that begins 5 days after reinstatement
An accident the day after reinstatement
questions.w: Accidents covered immediately; sickness after 10 days.

questions.q: Lena moves from office work to commercial fishing without telling her insurer. Under the change of occupation provision:
o: Benefits are reduced and the premium stays the same
questions.w: Riskier job → benefits reduced, premium unchanged.

questions.q: Jordan stated age 25 instead of 30 on a disability policy. The insurer will:
o: Reduce the benefit to what the premium buys at age 30
Raise the premium to the age-30 rate
questions.w: Course scenario: $500 benefit reduced to $400, same $100 premium.

questions.q: Which renewability provision lets the insurer raise rates only for an entire class, never change terms, and never cancel while premiums are paid?
questions.w: Guaranteed renewable: class-only premium increases.

questions.q: Which renewability type is most favorable to the insured and most expensive?
questions.w: Noncancelable: double guarantee, most expensive.

questions.q: A conditionally renewable policy may be terminated because the insured:
questions.w: Conditions like age or losing employment, never health.

questions.q: A policy is delivered March 3 with a 10-day free look. The last day to return it is:
questions.w: Day 1 = March 4, so day 10 = March 13.

questions.q: An insurer attaches a rider excluding any disability from the insured's right shoulder. This is a(n):
questions.w: Impairment (exclusion) rider.

questions.q: Under the pre-existing condition provision, insurers generally may not impose a waiting period longer than:
questions.w: Generally no more than 12 months.

questions.q: Mia and her husband each have their own employer group plan and are dependents on each other's plan. Their son's birthday is in June, Mia's is in April, and her husband's is in February. Whose plan is primary for the son?
questions.w: Birthday rule: husband's February birthday comes first.

questions.q: A 67-year-old employee works for a company with 50 employees and has the company's group plan. Which pays first?
questions.w: 20+ employees → employer plan primary, Medicare secondary.

questions.q: After paying a claim for injuries caused by a negligent driver, the insurer sues the driver to recover what it paid. This is:
questions.w: Subrogation.

questions.q: The insured and primary beneficiary die in the same car crash and no one can tell who died first. Under the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act, proceeds go to:
questions.w: Insured presumed to survive; paid to contingent.

questions.q: A common disaster provision typically requires the primary beneficiary to outlive the insured by:
questions.w: Typically 14–30 days.

questions.q: Which provision's name makes it sound mandatory even though it is optional?
questions.w: Conformity with state statutes is optional.

questions.q: Where are exclusions NOT found in a health policy?
questions.w: The exclusions section isn't on the policy face.

questions.q: Which premium mode costs the least overall?
questions.w: Annual is least expensive; monthly most.

questions.q: The owner's rights provision in a health policy lets the owner:
o: Transfer ownership freely, like life insurance
Assign benefit payments directly to providers
questions.w: Health owners can assign benefits but not transfer ownership.

questions.q: An irrevocable beneficiary:
o: Can be changed any time by the owner
Has no right to a copy of the policy
Must give written consent before the owner takes a policy loan or changes the beneficiary
questions.w: Vested interest; consent needed for loans, assignment, surrender, changes.

questions.q: The insurer discovers fraud on an application in year 4. Under the time limit on certain defenses:
o: The policy is incontestable after 3 years
Fraud overrides the time limit; the insurer may rescind
The insurer may only reduce benefits
The insurer must keep paying claims
questions.w: Fraud always overrides the time limit.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of underwriting, according to the course?
o: Protect the insurer against adverse selection
questions.w: Underwriting protects the insurer against adverse selection.

questions.q: Another term for underwriting is:
questions.w: Risk selection.

questions.q: Who performs field underwriting?
questions.w: The producer does field underwriting.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the agent's field-underwriting duties?
questions.w: The producer doesn't issue the policy.

questions.q: During pre-selection, an agent:
o: Cannot legally guarantee or bind coverage
questions.w: An agent can't legally guarantee or bind coverage.

questions.q: A non-medical application is most often used when the proposed insured:
o: Is older and wants high coverage
Is young and wants a low amount
questions.w: Low coverage, young applicant.

questions.q: Which part of the application must be completed in full on every application?
questions.w: Part II must be complete every time.

questions.q: The agent's report (Part III) is best described as:
o: A confidential communication between agent and insurer
questions.w: Confidential agent-to-insurer communication.

questions.q: A completed application plus the initial premium make up the applicant's:
questions.w: Exam Tip: application + initial premium = consideration.

questions.q: A misrepresentation is fraudulent when it is:
o: Material and made with fraudulent intent
questions.w: Material + fraudulent intent.

questions.q: A mother applies for and will own a policy on her 16-year-old son. Who signs?
questions.w: Third-party ownership: applicant, proposed insured, agent. Never the beneficiary.

questions.q: An applicant gave a wrong date. How is it corrected?
o: Agent corrects it and the applicant initials
questions.w: Agent corrects, applicant initials.

questions.q: A non-smoking, non-drinking applicant at a healthy weight is most likely:
questions.w: Preferred traits.

questions.q: In the course case studies, Robert (obese smoker, poorly managed diabetes, motorcycle racing) was rated up about:
questions.w: About 50% above standard, possibly with racing exclusions.

questions.q: An applicant works two jobs, one hazardous. Benefits and premiums are based on:
questions.w: Based on the more hazardous occupation.

questions.q: Which is a moral hazard, per the course?
questions.w: Moral hazards: drinking, drugs, poor credit, dishonest practices.

questions.q: Terminal illness and fraud are examples of which classification?
questions.w: Uninsurable examples in the quick-reference table.

questions.q: The formula for health insurance premiums is:
questions.w: Morbidity – Interest + Expenses.

questions.q: If an insurer assumes a higher interest rate on invested premiums, premiums will be:
questions.w: Higher assumed interest → lower premiums.

questions.q: A mutual insurer calls the profit built into its expense loading:
questions.w: Mutual companies call it surplus.

questions.q: An insured pays $240 in advance for a year and cancels after 3 months. The unearned premium refunded is:
questions.w: 9 of 12 months unearned: $240 × 9/12 = $180.

questions.q: Choosing a longer elimination period will make the premium:
questions.w: Longer elimination period → lower premium.

questions.q: In the Maria example, what was her final annual premium, and what did quarterly payment cost per year?
Setting the same rates for everyone in an area regardless of loss experience is:
questions.w: Community rating.

questions.q: Age aside, which statement is true according to the course?
o: Men pay more for health insurance
Women pay more for health insurance and men more for life
Women pay more for life insurance
questions.w: Women pay more for health, men for life.

questions.q: An application is submitted without the initial premium. It's called a:
questions.w: Trial application.

questions.q: Applicant signs Aug 2, takes a required exam Aug 4, and pays with the application, receiving an insurability-type conditional receipt. If found insurable, coverage starts:
questions.w: Later of the application date or required exam date.

questions.q: Under a conditional receipt, the applicant is found uninsurable. The result is:
questions.w: No coverage; premium refunded.

questions.q: Which receipt provides coverage only between approval/issue and delivery and is rarely used?
questions.w: Approval type; courts oppose it.

questions.q: A binding receipt:
o: Guarantees coverage until the insurer formally rejects the application
Is the most common receipt in health
questions.w: Coverage until formal rejection.

questions.q: The insurer offers coverage only at a rated premium. Legally, this is:
questions.w: The insurer rejects the offer and makes a counteroffer.

questions.q: Per the Exam Tip, coverage NEVER begins on:
questions.w: Never the issue date.

questions.q: The insurer mails a policy to the agent with instructions to deliver only if the applicant is still in good health. This is:
questions.w: A good-health condition means no constructive delivery.

questions.q: A question mentions a "premium receipt." Which can you rule out?
questions.w: Inspection receipts aren't premium receipts.

questions.q: Which document can designate the start of the free-look period?
questions.w: Delivery receipt.

questions.q: At delivery, the statement of good health shows a change in health. The agent should:
o: Report it to the company and not leave the policy
questions.w: Pending re-underwriting: report it, don't leave the policy.

questions.q: Which is true of the MIB?
o: Information is shared with any lender
Members report impairments by code number for underwriting and claims use only
questions.w: Code numbers; members only; underwriting and claims. MIB doesn't decide.

questions.q: An insurer that declines an applicant due to poor credit must notify them a copy is available from the credit bureau under the:
questions.w: FCRA.

questions.q: Insurers may not use genetic testing in health underwriting because of:
Which is a prohibited underwriting factor under unfair discrimination rules?
questions.w: Sexual orientation, religion, geographic location are prohibited.

questions.q: The Information and Privacy Protection Act prohibits insurers from:
o: Basing a decision solely on previous adverse underwriting decisions
questions.w: Can't rely solely on prior adverse decisions.

questions.q: The USA PATRIOT Act requires insurers to have:
questions.w: AML programs.

questions.q: An insurer routinely tests blood. It must still:
o: Get a signed HIV consent form
questions.w: HIV consent form required.

questions.q: In the Jennifer Chen case, she ended up classified as:
o: Standard with no rating or exclusions
questions.w: Standard, not preferred, no rating or exclusions.

questions.q: Who issues a certificate of authority to an insurer in Florida?
questions.w: OIR issues the COA (the Review Notes' "DFS" is the contradiction, #2).

questions.q: The Florida Insurance Commissioner is:
questions.w: Appointed by the FSC. Two deputies: P&C and L&H.

questions.q: An insurer formed under the laws of Georgia and selling in Florida is:
questions.w: Another U.S. state means foreign.

questions.q: An agent persuades a client to drop a policy and buy a new one from a different insurer by making a misleading comparison. This is:
questions.w: Different insurer = twisting. Same insurer = churning.

questions.q: Which gift to a prospect is NOT rebating?
o: A share of the agent's commission
questions.w: Gifts of $100 or less aren't rebating.

questions.q: What is the CE requirement every 2 years for an agent licensed less than 6 years?
questions.w: 20 electives + 4-hour update = 24 total.

questions.q: An agent moves their home address. They must notify DFS in writing within:
questions.w: 30 days. Fine up to $250 for a first offense.

questions.q: An insurer terminating an agent's appointment (not for cause) must give the agent at least:
questions.w: 60 days' advance notice unless for cause.

questions.q: An agent diverts $15,000 of premium. This is a:
questions.w: Over $300 and under $20,000 = 3rd-degree felony.

questions.q: The Florida Life and Health Insurance Guaranty Association pays up to how much for basic hospital, medical-surgical or major medical health benefits per life?
questions.w: $500,000 for basic hospital, medical-surgical, major medical (not LTC).

questions.q: Under Mini-COBRA, the qualified beneficiary must notify the insurer of the qualifying event within:
questions.w: 63 days. Then the insurer has 14 days and the beneficiary has 30.

questions.q: A Mini-COBRA beneficiary who is disabled may extend continuation to a total of:
questions.w: 18 + 11 = 29 months, at up to 150% premium.

questions.q: Under Florida law, to convert group health coverage to an individual policy, the person must have been insured under the group for at least:
questions.w: 3 months for health (6 months for group LTC).

questions.q: A child is covered under both parents' plans. Mom's birthday is March 10 (age 40); Dad's is January 5 (age 38). Which plan is primary?
o: Dad's, because his birthday comes first in the year
questions.w: Birthday rule: the earlier birthday in the calendar year, not age.

questions.q: An insurer decides to stop offering all health coverage in the large-group market. How much notice must it give?
questions.w: 180 days to leave a whole market. 90 days for one product.

questions.q: Which ad wording is prohibited for a hospital-confinement benefit policy?
o: "Benefits for each day you are hospitalized"
"Extra cash while you're in the hospital"
questions.w: "Tax-free," "extra cash," "extra income" and "extra pay" are banned.

questions.q: A Medicare supplement policy may limit coverage for a preexisting condition for no more than:
questions.w: 6 months.

questions.q: Which person may NOT buy a Medicare supplement?
o: A person enrolled in a Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan
A 65-year-old who just enrolled in Part B
A person replacing an existing Medicare supplement
questions.w: Medicare Advantage enrollees are ineligible. Replacement is allowed with notice.

questions.q: A long-term care policy's elimination period may NOT exceed:
questions.w: 180 days max. Prior hospitalization also can't be required.

questions.q: Which exclusion is NOT allowed in a Florida LTC policy?
o: Care provided by an immediate family member
questions.w: Mental and nervous disorders may be excluded, but not Alzheimer's.

questions.q: LTC insurers must offer inflation protection that increases benefits by at least:
questions.w: At least 5% compounded annually.

questions.q: An LTC policyholder with cognitive impairment misses a premium and the policy is canceled. Reinstatement is available for:
questions.w: 5 months for cognitive impairment, loss of functional capacity, or confinement over 60 days.

questions.q: A "small employer" under the Florida Employee Health Care Access Act has:
questions.w: 1 to 50 (Mini-COBRA's "fewer than 20" is a different law).

questions.q: Under the small employer law, an "eligible employee" works a normal week of at least:
questions.w: 25 hours.

questions.q: Which statement about a discount medical plan organization (DMPO) is true?
o: It is insurance regulated like an HMO
It is licensed by OIR but is not insurance
Its marketers must be licensed health agents
It must join the guaranty association
questions.w: Licensed by OIR, not insurance, and marketers need no agent license.

questions.q: Before testing an applicant for HIV, the insurer must:
questions.w: Written informed consent first.

terms.d: The transfer of risk through the pooling or accumulation of funds
The insurance company that provides coverage and assumes risk (also "insurance company" or "carrier")
The customer who receives protection under the policy
Authorized to solicit, sell, and transact coverage for specific insurers under an agent contract
Represents the insured (client), not the insurer, and cannot bind coverage
Anyone licensed to sell, solicit, or transact insurance: agents and brokers both
Owned by stockholders; typically issues nonparticipating policies
Owned by policyholders; typically issues participating policies with potential dividends
Owner can receive dividends and elect the board of directors
No dividends and no voting rights for the owner
Reviews applications, approves or declines coverage, assigns risk classifications
Processes, investigates, and pays claims
Restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss; the insured may not profit from a loss
Reimburses the actual loss: most accident, health, property, and casualty contracts
Pays a predetermined amount regardless of the actual loss: life insurance
Uncertainty regarding the possibility of loss
Only a chance of loss, no chance of gain. The only type that is insurable
Chance of loss or gain. Not insurable
Spreading the cost of possible losses over a large number of similar (homogeneous) exposure units
Higher-risk people seek or keep coverage more than lower-risk people. Also called selection against the insurer
The more similar, independent exposure units insured, the more closely actual losses match expected losses
Restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, with no profit or gain
The immediate, specific event or cause of a loss
Policy lists the perils it covers. Anything not listed is not covered
Policy covers all direct causes of loss except the perils it excludes
Unintended, unforeseen decrease in value due to a peril
Damage caused by a peril with no intervening cause. The peril is the proximate cause
A loss that results from a direct loss
Unforeseen, unexpected, unintended, sudden event at a specific time and place
Any event that causes a loss, including repeated or continuous exposure over time
A condition that increases the chance a peril will occur
Tangible condition you can see, measure or document (faulty wiring, high blood pressure)
Dishonest character or intentional acts (lying on an application, fraud)
Careless indifference because the insured has coverage (skipping preventive care)
Represents the **insurer** and is authorized to act on its behalf. Has a fiduciary responsibility to both the insurer and the policy owner.
Licensed producer who represents the **insured (client)**. Holds no appointments with insurers and **cannot bind coverage**.
Prepared by the insurer with no negotiation; applicant must "take it or leave it."
Items of value each party gives. Applicant: material information and premiums. Insurer: promise to pay covered claims.
Financial or economic interest in the subject of insurance; you would suffer a financial loss from its damage or loss.
A false statement that influences the insurer's decision to accept the risk, or the classification and pricing of the risk.
Both policy owner and insurer must disclose all material facts, with no attempt to conceal or deceive.
Never legally in force because it lacks an essential element.
May be set aside by one party for a reason satisfactory to the court.
The voluntary giving up of a known legal right.
The probability or risk of becoming ill or disabled
Only the **injury** must be unexpected and unintended, even if the act was intended. Less restrictive, most common, legally accepted
More restrictive: the **cause and the result** must both be unforeseen, unexpected and unintended
The **death benefit** paid under an AD&D policy
The lump sum paid for accidental **loss of sight or dismemberment** under AD&D
Disability credit insurance. Fixed end date; pays the monthly loan payment during disability; insurer exposure shrinks as the loan is paid down
Waiting period at the start of a disability or LTC claim before benefits begin. A deductible in time, not money
The list of medications a prescription drug plan covers
Review of whether proposed dental services are medically necessary and covered, the approved amount, and the patient's share. It does **not** authorize the procedure
Root canals; diseases of the tooth pulp
Gum disease diagnosis, treatment and prevention
Straightening teeth with braces and retainers
Dentures and other artificial dental devices
Extractions and other surgical treatment

Medical and dental: a plan that **reimburses** covered expenses. Disability, LTC and hospital indemnity: a **flat dollar amount** paid periodically (hospital indemnity and LTC pay it regardless of cost)

A self-funded employee welfare benefit plan contracts with an insurer (or independent TPA) for administration only. The plan stays responsible for claim costs; the insurer acts as a third-party administrator. Services: claims, Rx drug cards, COBRA administration, employee communications.
Service providers that pay participating providers directly. **Blue Cross = hospital** expenses; **Blue Shield = physician / surgical & medical** services. Members are called **subscribers**.
Payment **per patient, not per service**. HMO pays a flat amount per person. If the patient never uses care, the fee is "wasted" for the HMO; heavy use means the provider takes a loss.
A specialist inside the insurer (e.g., an RN) reviews potentially large claims as they develop and discusses treatment alternatives with the insured.
Given to each group participant ("evidence of insurance"). Participants are covered under one master contract and do **not** get separate policies.
Marriage, divorce, birth: lets a person buy/change coverage outside normal enrollment.
Providers deliver services inside HMO facilities (staff, group, network models).
Providers see members in their own offices, part-time (IPA model).
Employer with **20 or more** employees.
A **percentage** of costs, up to an annual maximum.
A **fixed dollar** amount per visit. Primary purpose: cover **administrative costs** (may also be cost sharing).
Small groups. Premium based on the surrounding community's claims experience and costs.
Large groups. Premium based on the group's own average number and cost of past claims.
Employees and employer share the premium.
Employer pays the entire premium.
Right to convert group coverage to an individual policy at termination, without evidence of insurability.

Prior coverage with **no break of 63 days or longer**. Reduces/eliminates a new plan's preexisting-condition waiting period. Includes individual major medical, group major medical, Medicaid, comparable plans, and COBRA coverage.
HMO approach for dental. A primary care dentist (PCD) manages care and refers. Copays, sometimes coinsurance. Sometimes called a prepaid plan.
**Not insurance.** Access to providers at discounted rates for a fee/dues. Typically regulated by the state department of insurance; some states may not permit them.
ERISA (1974)-compliant, employer-funded plan giving benefits other than pensions.
Limited window (typically once a year, a set number of days) to sign up. Most providers allow **31 days** for new eligibles.
Required when enrolling outside the enrollment period (late enrollees). Controls adverse selection.
Keeps paying an **existing** covered claim after the person is no longer eligible (fixed period or as long as the claim lasts). Does **not** cover new claims.
Coverage for association / professional society members who don't qualify for true group. **Individual policies** are issued; the association is only the sponsor; premiums typically discounted.

One master contract covering a group (employers, trade/professional associations, labor unions, credit unions). No individual underwriting / evidence of insurability for eligible members who enroll on time.
Comprehensive, **prepaid** plan that combines **financing and delivery** of care; emphasizes preventive care; fixed periodic fee instead of fee per service.
Traditional plan, no networks; reimburses the insured.
Issued to the sponsor (master policyholder), who is responsible for premiums. Contract is between insurer and sponsor.
Combines **10 or more** employers (per keywords) into one pool; the **MET holds the master contract**, not the employers. A fully insured MEWA set up by a third party (insurer or TPA).

Arrangement giving health/welfare benefits to employees of **2 or more unrelated employers** (ERISA §3(40)). Subject to ERISA and state law (except where state law conflicts with ERISA). Can be fully insured or self-funded.
A group that exists for a reason **other than obtaining insurance**.
HIPAA notice given at enrollment and at least **every 3 years** after.
Providers who contractually agree to specific fees (BC/BS).
HMO-like in-network care plus limited out-of-network coverage.
Sponsor contracts with a provider network at **prearranged discount prices**; fee-for-service.
Hybrid of HMO and PPO: no referrals needed for in-network specialists, but **no out-of-network coverage except true emergencies**.
Evaluation before a hospital stay for surgery to confirm it's medically necessary.
Amends the Civil Rights Act of 1964: pregnancy treated like any other condition for employment purposes.
The **gatekeeper** in HMOs and POS plans; controls referrals.
(1) Employment: waiting time before joining a group plan (often 1–3 months). (2) Policy: illness excluded (accidents covered) for 10–30 days after the policy is first in force.
Termination, disability, death, divorce, etc. (full list in Section 9).
Before admission / while care is provided / after treatment.
BC/BS: services from participating providers in exchange for premium.
Generally **2 to 50** full-time employees (30+ hrs/week); varies by state.
Bought by a self-funded employer; reimburses the employer when total claims exceed the risk retention limit (deductible). Best for large employers.
The minimum projected percentage of medical costs a policy is likely to cover
First-dollar benefits for specified, limited care; covers basic hospital, physician and surgical
Room and board, miscellaneous hospital expenses (lab, X-rays, medicines), operating room and supplies, up to a stated maximum
Surgeons' fees in or out of the hospital, plus anesthesiologist fees
A physician's non-surgical services
How long benefits are paid after a loss, or the policy period in which claims count toward limits
Employer benefit menu, including accident and health insurance, on a pre-tax basis
Claims in the final 3 months of a year, if the deductible wasn't met, count toward next year's deductible
The dollar value per unit in a relative value scale; change it to adjust the whole schedule
What the insured pays before the policy pays
10 benefits the ACA requires in major medical, with no lifetime or annual caps
Pays claims with no deductible
Federal website to check eligibility for government help and compare and buy plans
Major medical where the insured pays basic costs (except ACA preventive care) up to an annual out-of-pocket cap; IRS sets the limits for HSA use
Permanently excludes a condition disclosed on the application
Annual limits on specific covered services
The time before coverage starts in which a condition can be called pre-existing
Broad, high-benefit coverage for hospital, surgery and physician services with deductibles and coinsurance; meets ACA minimum essential coverage
Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum: the ACA coverage levels sold on exchanges
The most an insured pays for covered services in one plan year
Keeping access to group coverage when changing employers
A condition that exists before coverage starts, limited by law to one that showed up in a set period before
A temporary exclusion for undisclosed conditions treated during the look-back period; banned in ACA-qualifying policies
Basic surgical approach: a dollar value per unit, and a number of units per surgery
Originally the most coinsurance paid in a year; now used to mean the out-of-pocket maximum
Pays based on what is reasonable and customary in the geographic area where care was given

Both the **cause and the result** of the mishap must be accidental. Course example: Pedestrian A is accidentally bumped into the street by Pedestrian B and hit by a car. The cause and the result were both unintended, so it's covered.
Only the **result** has to be unexpected and unintended, even if the action was voluntary. **Far less restrictive** than accidental means.
Short-term extra benefit for the **first 6 to 12 months** of disability. It can add to employer benefits, pay early expenses, or fill the **5-month SSDI waiting period**.
Disabled if you can't do your own job **or any job you're reasonably suited for by education, training, or experience**.

terms.t: Any occupation for which the insured is reasonably suited
terms.d: In states that use this phrase, it means the same as "any occupation." In states that don't, "any occupation" is read more literally, so it's **stricter**.
Maximum time benefits are paid **per disability claim**. Longer benefit period = **higher premium**.
Reimburses the business for expenses and payroll if the owner is disabled. Does **not** replace the owner's income.
AD&D benefit for **dismemberment**. Typically **50% of the principal sum**.
AD&D benefit for **accidental death**. Equals the **face amount**.
Returns all premiums at **age 65**, less any benefits received. (Keyword page says "if no claims have been made.")
Switch to a **more hazardous** job: **benefit** is reduced. Switch to a **less hazardous** job: **premium** is reduced and excess unearned premium is refunded.
Several events cause the same disability, or one loss fits several definitions. **Only one benefit** is paid.
Insured must **stay indoors** (at home or in a hospital). Non-confined means they don't have to (e.g., doctor says to take walks).

Sets the order insurers pay. The primary pays as if it were the only carrier; the "contingent" coverage pays the remaining balance. **Group** disability benefits are reduced by Social Security and workers' comp.
Increases the benefit with the **CPI** to fight inflation, adjusted on each disability anniversary. Starts once a claim has been paid for **more than one year**. **Only found on LTD policies.**
Pays loan installments if the borrower is disabled. Pays the **creditor**, not the borrower. A form of **decreasing term disability**.

Covers a fixed period from issue, and the number of possible payments shrinks over time. Example: 5-year loan, disabled at end of year 1 = up to 4 years of payments; at end of year 4 = 1 year at most.
A total disability that shows up **later** after an accident. Policies allow a set window (20, 30, 60, 90 days, etc.).
Buy-sell agreement funded by disability insurance, used to buy out a disabled owner's share.
Pays **1% of the face amount** (up to $1,000) per month if the insured is totally disabled.
Optional **lump sum** instead of monthly payments for injuries named in the contract. Chosen when applying. Also used in buyout policies.
Time from the start of disability until benefits are payable. It's a **time deductible**. Longer elimination period = **lower premium**.
Payroll taxes paid by employees and employers that fund Social Security.
Benefit is a **fixed dollar amount**. Used mainly in **individual** policies.
Benefit is a **percentage of income** that adjusts as income changes. Used mainly in **group** policies.
SSA status for retirement and disability benefits. **40 quarters (10 years)** of FICA taxes = **permanent** fully insured. Younger workers need fewer quarters (sliding scale).

Right to buy more coverage at set future dates **without proof of good health**, as long as income has gone up. "**Use it or lose it**." Also called future increase option, additional purchase option, guaranteed purchase option.
Insurer must renew to the termination age if premiums are paid. Can't change policy terms but **can raise premiums by class**.
Insurer must renew **and** can't change the terms **or** the premium.
Extra benefit for each day in the hospital, on top of the monthly benefit.

terms.t: Impairment rider (exclusion rider, waiver for impairments)
terms.d: **Permanently excludes** certain losses so the insurer can still issue the policy, sometimes at a standard premium.
Defines disability purely as a **loss of income**.
Pays the **employer** if it loses a key employee's services.
Extends the benefit period **beyond age 65**.
**Monthly** payments, benefit period of **2 years or more**.
**Weekly** payments, benefit period of **no more than 2 years**. Group STD usually **26 weeks max**, integrated with sick time and LTD.
Requires an actual loss of income. If you can still earn as much as before, there's no loss and no claim.
The actual tasks you do on the job.
Your essential capabilities (also called "key duties").
The risk (likelihood) of becoming disabled. Considers personal and occupational factors.
A group formed for a legitimate purpose **other than buying group insurance**.
Pays medical costs up to a set amount for an injury that isn't disabling, if no other claim is filed. Requires proof of treatment.
Covers job-related **and** non-job-related disabilities: **24 hours a day, 7 days a week**.
Does **not** cover disabilities from the insured's employment (workers' comp handles those).
Disabled if you can't do the material and substantial duties of **your own** job.
Can't do **one or more (but not all)** key duties, or can't work your job **full-time**. Covered if income drops.
Proportional benefit when working less than full-time with an income loss of **at least 20%**.
Condition considered permanent (dismemberment, loss of sight, degenerative or chronic). Lump sum or weekly income.
Condition expected to be temporary unless re-evaluated at the end of the state's temporary benefit period.
Automatic total disability for **loss of 2 or more limbs**, or **permanent loss of sight, hearing, or speech**.
Basic Social Security monthly benefit, based on income and the taxes paid on it. **SSDI = 100% of PIA.**
One-time period at the **start** of the policy when **only accidents** are covered, not illness. Keyword page: **7 to 30 days**. Section 5.1.1: ends after **15, 30, or 60 days**.
Insurers share a claim in proportion to their share of the coverage. 60% of the coverage = pays 60% of the claim.
A relapse within the set period (**6 months**) is a continuation of the first claim: no new elimination period, no new benefit period.
Pays the approved cost of vocational training for a new occupation.
With multiple policies, total benefits **can't exceed income lost**. Each policy is reduced **pro rata**. Used by **individual** policies (group uses COB).

Refunds premiums if claims experience is favorable. Keyword page: dollar for dollar, **without interest**, if no claim is filed. Section 5.5.8: a percentage of premiums, at age 65 or every 5 or 10 years.

terms.t: Social Security rider (Social Insurance Supplement / Substitute, SIS)
terms.d: Pays a monthly benefit when Social Security (or workers' comp) is **delayed, denied, or less than the rider amount**.
The Social Security definition of disability. Replaced the older term **"any gainful work."**
Premiums are waived while the insured is disabled and receiving benefits (after the waiting period). **Not a loan.**
SSA's final test for SSDI: jobs exist in significant numbers, even outside your area of expertise or location, whether or not you'd be hired.
A form of **liability insurance** for workers hurt by work-related occurrences.

Pays part of a life policy's death benefit when the insured is diagnosed with a terminal illness (or other condition). Usually a **lump sum**. Amount paid is deducted from the death proceeds. **NAIC does not count it as LTC insurance.**
Provider accepts the **Medicare-approved amount as full payment** and won't bill the patient for more.
Six: **bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, eating**.

Care for seniors who live at home while the family caregiver is away or at work. Level of care is like home health care. Centers usually provide transportation. Can be medically based (PT) or recreation-based.

Residential community with **more limited services than a nursing home**. No around-the-clock care. Intermittent nursing (including medication management), housekeeping, meals, social activities. Someone needing help with **1 or 2 ADLs** may qualify.
Raises the LTC **stated daily benefit**, compounded annually, typically **5% per year**, often for a limited number of years. Cost is **built into the initial premium**.
Starts the day you're **admitted** to a hospital and ends **60 days after discharge**. Per claim, not per year.
How long benefits are paid for one claim: 12 months, 2, 3, 5, 10 years, or life. Minimum **1 year**. **3 years** is common.
Loss of **2 or more ADLs** or **cognitive impairment**. Either one qualifies.
"Choosing a Medigap Policy: A Guide to Health Insurance for People with Medicare," made by CMS and NAIC, updated yearly. Must be given **at the time of application**.
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid.
Deficiency in short or long-term **memory**; **orientation** to person, place, and time; deductive or abstract **reasoning**; or **judgment** about safety.
**Illegal**. Marketing that doesn't disclose that an agent may contact you to sell a policy.
Lets residents move from independent living to assisted living to an onsite skilled nursing home without leaving the community.
Built into **all tax-qualified LTC** policies. Triggered by a **"significant premium increase."** Owner can choose reduced coverage or paid-up options.
Benefits every Medigap plan must include (Plan A's benefits).

Help with personal needs (bathing, dressing, walking, eating, taking medication). Given by trained people who are **usually not medical personnel**, but it must be **ordered by a healthcare professional**.
**Illegal** to sell someone a second Medigap policy (other than a replacement).
Works like a deductible (as in disability income). Insured pays all costs until it ends. In LTC it often happens **only once**, because the condition usually isn't curable.
End-stage renal disease (kidney failure needing dialysis or transplant).
Paid care from professionals or aides. **Covered** by LTC.
Unpaid care by family. **Not covered**, but a policy may offer a **training allowance**.
A Part D plan's list of covered drugs, sorted by category and tier.
Lets the insured buy more coverage at set future times, at **attained age**, based on assumed inflation (generally **5%**), **without proof of insurability**.
Physical help with an ADL.
Caregiver is **within arm's reach** and can help if needed.
Either hands-on **or** stand-by assistance (NAIC definition).
**Illegal**. Selling through threats, excessive pressure, or fear.
**Personal care** at home: ADLs, meal prep, housework, transportation. Also called home setting or personal care.
Mostly **skilled** care at home, part-time (visiting nurses, medication, wound care, therapy ordered by a doctor).
Comfort care for the terminally ill (life expectancy **6 months or less**) at home or in a facility, instead of curative treatment.
Whole life or annuity combined with LTC. If no care is needed, you still get life or annuity benefits. Prioritizes LTC; must be underwritten.
**Intermittent** (occasional) nursing and rehab care by skilled personnel on a doctor's orders.
**60** extra hospital days usable once in a lifetime. **Not restored.**
Federally supported, **state-operated**. Buying a qualified partnership policy protects some assets from Medicaid spend-down. Must be **tax-qualified** and include **inflation protection**.
Private insurers contracted by region to process Original Medicare claims.
Private, Medicare-approved "all-in-one" plan that replaces Parts A and B.
A **Medigap** policy that uses a network (works like a closed-end HMO) in exchange for a **lower premium**.
Mailed **every 3 months**. Lists services billed, what Medicare paid, and what you may owe. **Not a bill.**
Private policy that fills gaps in **Original Medicare only**. Standardized lettered plans.
Give value if the policy lapses for nonpayment: reduced paid-up, shortened benefit period, return of premium.
Accepts assignment, bills Medicare directly. Balance billing is **strictly prohibited**.
Doesn't accept assignment. Can charge **up to 15% more** than the approved amount. Patient pays the provider and files with Medicare.
LTC total benefit is limited by **dollars, not days**. Cheaper care makes benefits last longer.
**Illegal**. Approving everyone and underwriting only when a claim comes in.
Short break for the unpaid family caregiver (overnight in-home stay, short facility stay, or adult day care).
Daily nursing and rehab by or under skilled medical staff, on a doctor's orders, **24 hours**, with periodic physician review.
LTC policy that meets **HIPAA** standards.
**Illegal**. Using misrepresentation to get someone to replace a policy.
The *Required Uniform Individual Accident and Sickness Policy Provisions Law*. Nearly all states adopted it or something similar. Sets consistent wording for **individual** health contracts.
Must be in all individually underwritten contracts. Protect the **insured**. Not specific to any one type of policy.
Protect the **insurer**. Define the insurer's rights and so limit them. Some apply only to certain policies (e.g., relation of earnings in disability). States may modify them.
All 23 are in standard wording. An insurer may use its own wording only with state approval, and it can't be **less favorable** to the insured.
Assignee gets full control of the policy and full rights to its benefits.
Pays an extra sum to the beneficiary if the insured dies in a covered accident, often a multiple of the face amount.
Pays part of the death benefit before death if the insured is terminally ill.
Contract = policy form + signed application + attachments (riders, endorsements).
Incontestability. After a set period, the insurer can't contest application statements. Fraud always overrides it.
Time after the due date when premium can be paid with no lapse: 7 / 10 / 31 days.
Puts a lapsed policy back in force (evidence of insurability + past-due premium, per keywords).
Insured tells insurer of a loss: 20 days.
Insurer must send forms within 15 days of notice.
Insured proves the loss: 90 days (up to 1 year if legally incapable).
Days after delivery to return the policy for a full refund: typically 10 (30 for direct mail and Medicare supplements). Also called "right to examine."
The insurer's promise: types of benefits, when paid, start date and end of term.
The insured's side of the exchange: **premium** + **statements on the application**.
Can't be canceled, terms can't change, premium can't rise while premiums are paid. Most expensive. Renewable to a stated age.
Can't be canceled or changed while premiums are paid, but premium **can** rise for an **entire class**.
Also called exclusion rider, coverage waiver, waiver of disability. Restricts coverage for a specific illness/injury for years or for life.
No coverage for conditions that existed before the policy's effective date.
Illness not covered for a short time after the policy starts or is reinstated. Accidents covered right away.
Stops duplicate payment when someone has more than one **group** plan. Total paid can't exceed allowable expenses.
Insurer pays its insured, then sues the at-fault third party to recover what it paid.
Insurance restores ("makes whole") the insured to their pre-loss financial position, with no profit.
Revocable: owner can change anytime without telling them. Irrevocable: needs their **written consent**; has a vested interest.
Evaluating applications to decide **insurability** and the right **premium** for the risk. Also called **risk selection**.

The tendency of **higher-risk (poorer) risks** to seek coverage, or the chance an insurer accepts bad risks (poor health, moral hazards). "Those most likely to have a loss are most likely to seek insurance." Underwriting exists to **protect the insurer against it**.
The **first step**, done by the **producer/agent**: screening, gathering information, submitting applications.
The underwriter's **principal tool** and **primary source**; reviewed **first**. Also the applicant's formal request for insurance.
Detailed report from the doctor who treated the applicant, requested when the medical section raises questions about a **specific condition**. Needs a copy of the **signed authorization**.
Industry database, formed by **700+** member insurers, of **coded** medical information. Helps prevent **fraud and misrepresentation**. Does **not** make underwriting decisions.
Risk of **illness or disability** in a defined population. Morbidity tables show the **frequency, extent and duration** of disability expected in a group.
Periodic payment to keep a policy in force, **always paid in advance**.
Sorting applicants into **preferred, standard, substandard** (or declined) by likelihood of claims.
Answers true **to the best of the applicant's knowledge and belief**. Not warranted exact in every detail; must be accurate as far as **material** to the risk.
Habits or lifestyle that signal extra risk: excessive drinking, drug use, poor credit, dishonest business practices.
Another word for **hobbies**.
Applicant would **suffer a loss** if the insured has medical expenses or can't work. A **prerequisite** for issuing a health policy.
Prorated part of paid-in-advance premium the insurer has "earned" by already providing coverage.
Prorated part not yet earned. A **liability** on the insurer's balance sheet, **refunded if the policy is canceled**.
Small transaction fee charged in addition to premium, paid annually or once at issue.
The "expenses" part of the premium formula: commissions, wages, admin, overhead, required reserves, and **profit** (called **surplus** by mutual companies).
Same rate structure for everyone in a community regardless of past or potential losses; used for **small groups and individuals**.
Group health premiums based on the **group's own claims experience**.
Coverage as of the application date (or medical exam date, whichever is later) **if** the applicant proves insurable. Also called a **temporary receipt**. Most common.
Coverage **guaranteed until the insurer formally rejects** the application, even if the applicant is uninsurable. Also called **temporary insurance agreement** or **unconditional receipt**.
Application submitted **without** the initial premium.
Legal delivery without physical delivery: the insurer gives up all control of the policy (e.g., mails it to the agent for **unconditional** delivery).
Signed when the applicant reviews the policy **before** paying. **Not** a premium receipt.
Signed when premium is collected at delivery: health hasn't changed since the application or exam.
Signed by the insured on receiving the policy; proof of delivery that can **start the free-look period**.
Summarizes the policy's **benefits and limitations**; most states require it for each applicant.
Generic NAIC publication explaining insurance in general terms; doesn't address the specific policy. Required in some sales, e.g., **long-term care**.
Describes the **specific** product: agent, insurer, policy, riders, premiums, benefits, etc.
In Florida: a general lines, life, health or title agent. Includes "producer." It does **not** include customer representatives, limited customer representatives or service representatives.
A business location where insurance transactions that only licensed agents can do take place. Each location needs an **agent in charge**.
Licensed to sell, solicit or negotiate insurance for compensation. Also called agent or broker.
Solicitation or inducement, preliminary negotiations, effectuation, and handling matters afterward. Servicing counts too.
Trying to persuade someone to buy: describing benefits, terms or premiums; handing out an invitation to contract; making recommendations; completing applications; comparing or interpreting products.
Every person engaged as indemnitor, surety or contractor in the business of insurance or annuities.
Insurance for insurance companies. The **ceding** insurer passes risk to the **reinsurer** for more capacity and stability.
Formed under Florida law / formed in another U.S. state or territory / formed in another country.
Incorporated society for members and beneficiaries only. No capital stock, not for profit, lodge system with ritualistic work, representative government.
The insurer's "business license," issued by **OIR**, to transact insurance in Florida.
Has a COA from OIR.
No COA. Denied, or never applied.
Owned by stockholders. Generally nonparticipating. Goal is profit for owners.
Owned by policyowners. Participating, pays dividends. Goal is the lowest net cost.
A stock company that issues both participating and nonparticipating policies.
A position of trust. Florida agents are fiduciaries: they collect, record and remit premiums. The application page adds that it means acting in the **customer's best interest**.
All premiums, return premiums and other funds an agent receives are held in a fiduciary capacity.
Mixing insurer money with personal or agency money. A breach of fiduciary duty.
Insurance written on the agent's own life, health, property, immediate family or business associates. Generally limited to **50%** of sales.
Giving anything of value not stated in the policy to induce a purchase. Gifts of **$100 or less** are not rebating.
Misrepresenting to get someone to drop a policy and buy one from **another insurer**.
The same misrepresenting behavior, but with policy values used to buy from the **same insurer**.
Telling a buyer that extra coverage is legally required or free when it isn't, or charging for it without consent.
Physical or mental force to make someone buy.
Knowingly making or spreading false or maliciously critical statements meant to injure a person.
Self-appoints. Has no insurer appointment. Advises for a fee set in advance by a written contract.
Authority from an insurer or employer to transact insurance on its behalf.
A third party that takes control to rehabilitate or liquidate an insurer. In Florida that's **DFS**.
Not insolvent, but the Department thinks it may be unable to meet its obligations.
A court has issued an order of liquidation with a finding of insolvency.
Health plan someone was enrolled in on **March 23, 2010**, covering them continuously since. Doesn't have to meet every ACA rule.
A provider charging the insured the difference between what the insurer pays and what the provider charges.
The Florida Health Insurance Coverage Continuation Act. Covers employees of small employers (**fewer than 20**) that federal COBRA doesn't reach.
The covered employee (unless fired for gross misconduct), spouse or dependent child, judged the day before the qualifying event.
Required in group hospital, medical and surgical expense policies. Insurers together can't pay more than 100% of reasonable expenses.
A summary of a policy's main benefits, exclusions and renewal terms, given at the time of application.
A consumer guide. Medicare supplement uses a Buyer's Guide; LTC uses the NAIC Shopper's Guide.
Certified as unable to do at least **2 ADLs** for at least **90 days**, or needing substantial supervision because of severe cognitive impairment.
Bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, eating (6).
A deficiency in short- or long-term memory, orientation to person, place and time, deductive or abstract reasoning, or judgment about safety.
A policy that must be offered regardless of health status, preexisting conditions or claims history.
Spreads risk across a geographic area but allows separate factors for age, gender, family composition and tobacco use.
Enrolls outside the first eligibility period or a special enrollment period.
Discount medical plan organization. Licensed by OIR but **not insurance**. Marketers don't need an agent license.
